summary: Trajectory-ΔV is a browser game where players design a whole space mission to the Moon or Mars. They pick a world, a ready-made rocket, a spacecraft, power, instruments and a radio, and six live meters (budget, weight, power, data link, lifetime, science) show the cost of every choice. Pressing Launch plays the mission: liftoff, the trip, the braking burn, then months of science with random events such as solar storms and radio dropouts. A report gives stars and a score and explains why the mission worked or failed. Players can then fly the same missions with real physics, from a first launch to Moon landings, Mars and Voyager.
details: Trajectory-ΔV is a space mission design game that runs in the browser, built to answer the Space Mission Design Game challenge. It has two connected parts. 1. Mission Control (design and operate a mission). The player picks a world to explore (watch Earth's weather, map the Moon, watch the Sun, or explore Mars). Six round tools open the choices: orbit, rocket (ready-made launch vehicles drawn to scale, with the cheapest one that fits tagged), spacecraft (body, engine, safety extras), power (solar arrays, battery), science (11 instruments with mass, power, cost, data and science value) and radio plus mission length. Six live meters show budget, weight vs the rocket's capacity, power, data link, lifetime and projected science, so every choice has a visible consequence: a better camera weighs more, needs more power and makes more data than the radio can send. A one-tap ready-made mission per world helps beginners; four difficulty levels and a team mode (four roles on one screen: mission lead, spacecraft engineer, science lead, operations lead) add depth. Pressing Launch plays the mission: liftoff, the trip to the Moon or Mars, the braking burn, then months of science with random events (solar storms, instrument glitches, radio dropouts, debris, ground outages). The report gives stars and a score, explains in plain words why the mission worked or fell short, and suggests what to try next. Designs can be shared as a code, and the best scores are kept in a local leaderboard. 2. Missions (fly it yourself). Ten missions get harder in order: reach space, reach orbit, raise an orbit, Moon flyby, lunar orbit, Moon landing, return and re-entry, then three special missions: the full Apollo-style round trip, Mars (launch window, cruise, orbit, entry, parachute, landing) and Voyager (a 1977 launch window and Jupiter's gravity bending the path to Saturn). Players choose Watch (autopilot), Fly with help (prompts) or Fly it yourself. A rocket builder with ready-made rockets, three tutorials, a sandbox and a Milky Way explorer with 4,834 real planet-hosting stars complete it. How it uses NASA data: planet and Moon mass, radius, gravity, atmosphere and orbit come from the NASA NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheets and JPL Solar System Dynamics. The Milky Way explorer draws star positions from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Planet textures are NASA imagery. Mission facts and lesson text cite NSSDCA and NASA Science pages. Every value in the mission data files carries a source or is marked simplified. Tools: React, three.js and Vite (JavaScript), IBM Plex fonts. Built with Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding assistant), directed and reviewed by the team. Honest limits: the flight model is simplified on purpose (flat 2D orbits, circular planet orbits, simple atmosphere). The Studio's rocket, spacecraft and instrument figures are rounded teaching values, not data for any real vehicle, and are marked simplified. Team mode is pass-and-play on one screen: there is no online multiplayer, and the leaderboard is stored on the player's own device. Not built yet: onboard computer and attitude control as separate parts. Built by Medhansh Negi and Jay Raj Sharma on November 14-15, 2026. Open source under the Apache License 2.0.
